chapter_theme: Questions about origins (where did form arise in the matchless light, where does the mind rise, sleep and go astray) are answered by turning worship inward: the body is the shrine where the Lord is seen, mind is the flower and water, the breath is the smith's bellows that blows the light into a blaze. Temple and mosque, homa pit, Vedas and bound books come to nothing once the Lord is known; what remains is the one, the one letter, bindu and nada, and the refrain Sivayam.
structure_note: A running cut of one editorial heading (அறிவு நிலை), not an arranged chapter. Runs within it: a series of questions on where form, worlds and mind stand (1139 to 1142); the yoga of root fire, nectar and the dance at the crown (1143, 1144); the one and the uselessness of scripture (1145, 1146); the body as shrine and alchemical blowing (1147 to 1149); the silent yogi and the apophatic one (1150, 1151); ladders of letters (1152, 1153); jibes at Brahmin birth and false puja (1154 to 1158); and the inner body, sun and moon, root circle and seed as the mantra's seat, closing with the heart as the temple (1159 to 1163).

1139.reading: Where is the place where form arose within the incomparable great light? Where did it, becoming comparable, pierce through the cosmos? Where did the Supreme, who is austerity itself, stand bearing a form? Where did water, born in the Supreme, stay?
1139.nuance: Four questions on how the formless took form, with no answer. உவமையிலா (without compare) and உவமையாகி (becoming comparable) mark the step from the unmanifest to the manifest; சலம், water, is the first of the elements to be asked about, perhaps as the womb's water or the first fluid of creation.

1140.reading: Where did three bulls calve a single calf in the sky? Tell me where the seven lower worlds stand. From the play of him and her the rare Siva was born, and she herself is Meru: where is that?
1140.nuance: Riddles. Three bulls birthing a calf is an impossible image; tradition takes the bulls as the three channels or three gunas and the calf as the breath or the inner light. Siva born from the play of him and her inverts the usual order and may mean the Siva-state in the yogi; Meru as 'she' is, in body-cosmos reading, the spine. The last words (அவமைதானது) are garbled, perhaps உவமை (likeness).

1141.reading: Where does it stand to rise, where to subside? Where does it move, where is the eye's sleep? Where does it stand to think, and where is the mind's confusion? Jnanis who are able to lay down the rule must explain this at length.
1141.nuance: The subject that rises, subsides, moves, sleeps, thinks and is confused is unnamed; the mind and the breath both fit, and the Siddhars treat them as one movement. The verse asks the jnanis, not the books, to answer, and asks for length (விரிந்து), which the poet's own four lines never give.

1142.reading: Eight gates that turn and play, eight gates that are proclaimed, eight shapes without sides, eight gates where fire plays, eight shapes without a straw in them: you deluded ones who went round and round them! There is also a flower that never budded; by the Lord's oath it is true.
1142.nuance: Five eights, which tradition spreads over the eight directions, the eight siddhis, the eight-petalled lotus and the eightfold yoga; the mapping cannot be fixed from the stanza. The flower without a bud (அரும்பிலாத பூ) is the clearest line: a thing with no origin, the Lord or awareness itself, set against all the eights the deluded circle.

1143.reading: Staying put, kindling the root fire's heat with the breath, so that the honey's chamber opens and one sweetness is tasted; with the three moons from the sky entered into the staff: the yogi who takes this measure while still in the flesh is a yogi indeed.
1143.nuance: The sequence is the standard one of Siddhar yoga: breath heats the fire at the root, the nectar's chamber (தேன் அறை) in the head opens, and sweetness is tasted. மதியம் மூன்று (three moons) and தண்டலம் (the staff's ground, taken as the spine) are the coded terms; the three may be the three kalas of the moon or three centres. ஊனிருந்து, 'while in the flesh', insists that the measure is taken in this body.

1144.reading: When one is thought of as freed, at the crown of the finished cosmos the Father and the Mother danced together in love. You jnanis and siddhas who speak of the dance at Tillai: when the Father's dance began, all things took up the dance.
1144.nuance: பத்தனார் in line 2 is probably அத்தனார் (the Father), as line 4 has அத்தன். The dance is moved from the hall at Tillai (Chidambaram) to the crown of the cosmos, which in body-cosmos reading is the crown of the head; the address to siddhas who 'say Tillai' is a jibe at those who locate it in a town. அடங்கல் ஆடல், the whole dancing, may mean all things joined the dance or that the dance is the end (அடங்கல்) of all.

1145.reading: One, and one, and only one: the whole world is one, then and now it is one, the beginningless is one. Cut the tarnish from the hardened red gold and set it true, and that day you will know the god within yourselves: Sivayam.
1145.nuance: ஒன்று is said eight times in two lines. The second half gives the method: the tarnish (களிம்பு) is what hides the one; the gold is not made, only cleaned. உம்முளே places the god within the hearers, so the oneness is also between them and him.

1146.reading: The planted images, the shastras recited, the homa pit set up to one's liking, the four Vedas in concord, the books tied up in bundles, all that fierce babbling: it all ended as nothing once I knew the Lord.
1146.nuance: தாவரம் (the immovable) may be planted trees or installed images; the list runs from stone to fire to text. பொட்டதாய் முடிந்ததே, 'ended as a dot', is finality rather than refutation: the poet does not argue with scripture, he reports that it dropped away. The first person (பிரானை யான் அறியவே) is rare in these stanzas.

1147.reading: In the round cage the moon grew and rose; close by its frame stood conch and discus; when the axle slipped and the door at the gate was shut, how did the Siva who had risen within the egg get out?
1147.nuance: A riddle on the body as egg and cage. The moon in the round cage is, by tradition, the nectar or the mind in the skull; conch and discus are Vishnu's emblems, here perhaps the two side channels or the ears and eyes; the axle (அச்சு) the spine or the breath. The question is how the indwelling Siva, or the soul, leaves at death once the gates are shut, and the stanza does not answer it.

1148.reading: What is a temple, what a palli, what is the spot you have marked out? What are the mantras you stand mouthing in worship? Bow rightly in the shrine of wisdom and you will see the Lord in the shrine of the body.
1148.nuance: பள்ளி is the word for Jain and Buddhist shrines and for mosques, as well as for schools; set beside கோயில் it levels the sects' houses together. The answer keeps the word and moves it: the palli of wisdom and the palli of the body (ஞானமான பள்ளி, காயமான பள்ளி). The mantras are faulted as spoken 'with the mouth' (வாயினால்), not as mantras.

1149.reading: Good silver counted six, fine copper four, killing lead three, bright red gold two, with the bow-string's sound one: if you can blow so that these shine, the light itself can be made into gold of the eighth touch.
1149.nuance: An alchemical stanza read by tradition as yoga: the metals are the body's elements or states, ஊதல் (blowing) is breath-control, and எட்டு மாற்று is both the purest touch of gold and 'to reach' (எட்ட). நாகம் may be lead, as in alchemy, or the serpent. The counts six, four, three, two, one are not explained. The verse makes a claim about transmutation and leaves the procedure, if there is one, unsaid; it is read here for what it claims, not as a recipe.

1150.reading: Yogis of silent wisdom whose inner dirt is uncut stay dirty though they live in the forest; yogis of silent wisdom who have cut the dirt within have cut off birth, though they sit among corpses.
1150.nuance: The same title, மவுன ஞான யோகிகள், is given to both kinds, so silence and the forest are not what divide them; மனத்தகத்து அழுக்கு, the dirt in the mind, is. பிணத்தடம், a place of corpses, is the cremation ground where Siddhars sat, chosen as the least pure place to make the point.

1151.reading: Not form and not light, it stood as one; not scent and not smell, not reached by the slow channel; not large, not small, not even the speaking breath: who can see the rare straightness that stands?
1151.nuance: An apophatic stanza, denying even light (ஒளியும் அல்ல) after many stanzas that make the Lord light. மந்த நாடி, the slow channel, is unclear, perhaps a nadi of the body or dull inquiry. நேர்மை (straightness, rightness) is the poet's word for what remains when all is denied; 1160 uses it for the line beyond sun and moon.

1152.reading: In the one letter from which the whole world rose, in the two letters whose spoken joy you do not know, in the three letters that rose as the three gods, in the four letters spoken on the tongue: Sivayam.
1152.nuance: A ladder of mantras by letter-count, ending at the refrain, which has four syllables (சி-வா-ய-ம்). The one letter is Om or the letter A; the two are, in tradition, the breath's unspoken syllables (ஹம்ஸ or சோகம்); the three are அ உ ம, read as the trimurti; the four are the refrain itself, so the stanza ends by naming its own closing word as the mantra. These identifications are the tradition's; the verse gives only the counts.

1153.reading: Beginning and end, the root bindu and nada became the five elements; the root bindu and nada became the five letters; the root bindu and nada stood pervading all; the root bindu and nada are themselves Sivayam.
1153.nuance: The first three words of every line are the same, and the stanza is a formula: bindu and nada, the first pair of Saiva cosmology, become elements, letters and pervasion in turn, and are then identified with the refrain. ஆதி அந்தம் (beginning and end) makes them both the first and the last.

1154.reading: All who gave food will live for many crores; all who gave gold may hold lordship; all who gave ... will fall into the hot hell; and all who 'broke in' will surely stand beyond.
1154.nuance: The first two lines are ordinary merit-talk; the last two are not. விண்ணம் is obscure (an ulcer? a corrupt word?) and what sends to hell is lost with it. கன்னம் இட்ட is housebreaking, and that burglars go beyond is either Siddhar irony or code: the one who breaks into the inner house, the thief who knows the theft of 1167. Another reading hears கர்ண (the ear) and takes it as those who received the whispered initiation.

1155.reading: You who stand beyond all recitation, free of sleep and food, free of caste difference, standing without doubt, knowing the intent within faultless understanding, standing with nothing at all: how is it that you move?
1155.nuance: நீர் (you) is not identified: the Lord, who has no caste or need, or the jnani who has reached that state. The list of absences, no recitation, no sleep, no caste, no doubt, no thing, suits either, and the final question (இயங்குமாறு எங்ஙனே?) is the same one asked of the formless Lord's action in Siddhanta.

1156.reading: When you were born, did the loincloth, the shining thread and the tuft come born with you, and all the bundle of bright threads? Did the four forgotten Vedas rise in your mind? What can you say, you who stand with the earth split and the sky fallen?
1156.nuance: The argument from birth: nothing a Brahmin is marked by was present at birth, so none of it is nature. மறந்த நாலு வேதம், the forgotten Vedas, may mean the Vedas no one remembers from a past life, or Vedas learned and forgotten. The last line's split earth and fallen sky is the collapse of the claim, not a cosmic event.

1157.reading: The bellows is there, the smith is there, the golden light is there; if you can think with a mind set right and blow so that it shines, the great pillar will blaze and spread as a mass of flame, and nothing remains but the dancing light and you.
1157.nuance: The smithy is the body: the bellows the breath, the smith the practitioner or the Lord, the pillar the spine or the flame-linga. The verse answers 1149's 'if you can blow' with what the blowing is for, and its end is not gold but a light that dances (நிருத்தமான சோதி) and a 'you' left standing with it.

1158.reading: Dressed in your guise, polishing the vessels, with heaps of incense and lamps, you behave like men who have butchered a goat and shared out the pieces; you spread out all the copper you could hunt up in heaps and throw flowers at it: what kind of worship is that?
1158.nuance: The priests arranging their copper vessels and images are likened to butchers dividing a carcass; the comparison may also recall 1122's sacrifice. மின் துலக்கி is 'polishing to a shine' (the brass), or 'polishing lightning'. The copper that is 'hunted up' (தேடிவந்த) suggests the images are collected goods.

1159.reading: If you can look past the place where you stand clutching the life that sprouted from the womb's impurity, then the Lord who stands at the crown, beyond blame and beyond pointing, becomes the house in which you dwell, with hands reaching the eight directions.
1159.nuance: முட்டுகண்ட தூமை is hard: the impurity that is blocked (the menses stopped at conception) or that is met with. திட்டும் அற்று சுட்டும் அற்று, without blame and without pointing, denies the Lord both censure and reference. முடியில் நின்ற நாதன் is the Lord at the crown of the head, and the house (வீடு) is also release.

1160.reading: Sun and moon, and beyond them the crowding stars that press upward: those who can melt that straight line into the one letter, in the incomparable void, and stay there, are not born again.
1160.nuance: The gloss fixes அருக்கன் and சோமன் as sun and moon, and in yogic tradition they are the right and left channels, so 'beyond them' is the middle way or the crown. தாரகை (star) may be the third light that arises when fire joins sun and moon, as Tirumular has it, or the bindu. The one letter is Om; உருக்கி (melting) treats it as metal, as in 1145 and 1149.

1161.reading: You who stood shaken and tossed on the three ornate circles above the five letters that sprout from the root circle: if that becomes the wisdom spoken in the hall of the leaf-circle, it stands as the fragrant circle, Sivayam.
1161.nuance: வட்டம் (circle) ends the first word-group of every line. The root circle is the muladhara; the three circles above it are, by tradition, the mandalas of fire, sun and moon or three centres; ஓலை வட்ட மன்று (the hall of the leaf-circle) and ஏல வட்டம் (the fragrant circle) are not fixed. The plain claim is that the body's circles become wisdom only when spoken in the hall, that is, when the dance is known.

1162.reading: In the region of the seed, at the doorway of the blood, within the eight pearl-strings in the chamber of the root centre, in the fearless membrane, as Hari, Hara and Brahma: the mantra that is uttered there is truly Sivayam.
1162.nuance: The body's generative places (சுக்கிலம் the seed, சுரோணிதம் the blood) are made the seat of the mantra and of the three gods, so the lowest centre is where the five letters sound. முத்துசரம் எட்டு, eight pearl strings, may be eight channels or the petals of a lotus; அச்சமற்ற சவ்வு, the fearless membrane, is obscure.

1163.reading: Flower and water are my mind, my heart the temple where he fits; the breath runs as the linga, though he fills the whole universe; the five senses that come are the shining incense and lamp; and for the dancing Lord there are no dusk-and-dawn hours.
1163.nuance: Each item of puja is matched to a part of the person, as in Tirumanthiram 1823, and the senses (ஐவர், the five) become the lamp rather than the enemy. The last line denies appointed hours (அந்தி சந்தி) to the Dancer, which cuts the timed rites of the twilight prayers; whether the poet denies them any value or only says inner worship is continuous is left open.

links.note: Both count the body's gates in cipher. Tirumanthiram 457 has eight that go out, eighteen that come in and nine gates, with the serpent and four horses; 1142 has five sets of eight gates and shapes that the deluded circle. Neither count is explained in its stanza, and the two do not match, which shows the cipher was not a fixed code even between parent and child text.

Tirumanthiram 669 says the fire at the root of the central channel drives the sun and lets the moon drink, and the siddhis follow. 1143 has the yogi kindle the root fire (மூல அங்கி) with the breath so that the honey's chamber opens and the moons enter the staff. The same sequence of root fire, breath and nectar is the mark of the good yogi in both; Tirumular ends in powers, Sivavakkiyar in a 'measure taken in the flesh'.

Tirumanthiram 2962 says 'see, there is one God for the world', and tastes the fruit நமசிவாய. 1145 says one and only one, the whole world is one, and ends in the refrain சிவாயம். Both tie the oneness to the five-letter mantra; Sivavakkiyar adds that the one is found by cleaning the self like gold.

Tirumanthiram 214 says that when steadfast Brahmins pour the oblation, sky and earth, the quarters, the gods and great wealth all flourish: the homa sustains the world. 1146 says the homa pit (ஓமகுண்டம்), with Vedas, shastras and books, is fierce babble that came to nothing once the Lord was known. The conflict holds on the plain reading of each; it softens only if 1146 means the rite is empty for the knower alone and 214 speaks of the land at large.

Kural 34 says that to be spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and all else is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர). 1146 calls installed images, homa, Vedas and bound books fierce babbling (கடும்பிதற்று) that ended as nothing when the Lord was known. Both dismiss outward religion as noise; the Kural's standard is a clean mind, Sivavakkiyar's a knowing of the Lord.

Tirumanthiram 2614 says he is not in the mansion, the hall, the courtyard, the temple or the holy garb, but in the hidden place in the heart of those who have given up longing. 1148 asks what temple or palli is, and says the Lord is seen in the shrine of the body by one who bows in the shrine of wisdom. Both deny the Lord to the building and give him to the inner person; Sivavakkiyar names the mosque or Jain shrine alongside the temple.

1148 says the Lord is seen in the shrine of the body (காயமான பள்ளி) when one bows in the shrine of wisdom. 1163 builds that shrine item by item: mind as flower and water, heart as the temple, breath as the linga, the five senses as incense and lamp, and no fixed hours. The second stanza furnishes what the first only named.

Both turn on ஊத வல்லீரேல், 'if you can blow'. 1149 lists metals by number and promises gold of the eighth touch; 1157 names the bellows, the smith and the golden light and promises a pillar of flame and a dancing light with 'you' left beside it. Read together, the alchemy of 1149 is given its yogic sense in 1157: the blowing is breath, the gold is light.

Tirumanthiram 1611 says that for those to whom silence has come, release comes and the powers stand before them. 1150 says silent-wisdom yogis whose inner dirt is uncut stay dirty even in the forest, and only those who have cut it have cut off birth. Sivavakkiyar grants silence its name but denies that it does anything by itself; the mind's dirt, not the vow, decides.

Tirumanthiram 1437 defines the attainment of Siddhanta as being neither one nor two nor nothing, yet one, and leaving the sects and the formless. 1151 denies form, light, scent, size and even the speaking breath, and asks who can see the rare straightness that stands as one. Both reach the one by denials, and both deny even the categories a devotee would hold on to (form, light).

Kural 1 makes the letter A the first of all letters as the Lord is the first of the world. 1152 begins with the one letter within which the whole world rose (ஓரெழுத்து உலகெலாம் உதித்த அட்சரம்). Both ground the world in a first letter; the Kural uses it as a comparison, Sivavakkiyar as the first rung of a mantra ladder that ends in his own refrain.

Tirumanthiram 966 says that by the five letters the Lord made the five elements, the wombs of birth and the world, and by them stands seated. 1153 says the root bindu and nada became the five elements and the five letters and stood pervading all. Both make the five syllables and the five elements two forms of one making; Sivavakkiyar names bindu and nada as the source where Tirumular names the Lord.

Tirumanthiram 230 asks whether thread and tuft are Brahman, answers that the thread is cotton and the tuft hair, and gives the true thread as Vedanta and the true tuft as knowledge. 1156 asks whether loincloth, thread and tuft were born with the Brahmin, and whether the Vedas rose in his mind at birth. Both strip the emblems of any natural standing; Tirumular keeps them as signs of something inner, Sivavakkiyar offers no replacement.

Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns. 1156 says the loincloth, thread and tuft did not come with birth, so they are not what a Brahmin is. Both deny that outward marks make the religious man; the Kural speaks of the ascetic's hair, Sivavakkiyar of the Brahmin's thread, and the Kural supplies a conduct test where Sivavakkiyar supplies none.

Tirumanthiram 820 says that if the breath rises swiftly inside the body, the temple daubed with black is lit with a gem lamp. 1157 says that if one blows the bellows with a right mind, the great pillar blazes and spreads, and only the dancing light and 'you' remain. In both the rising breath lights the dark body; Tirumular's figure is a lamp in a temple, Sivavakkiyar's a smith's fire.

Tirumanthiram 1837 says those who strew great flowers and cry 'our Lord's red feet' never come to know the holy one. 1158 says those who spread out heaps of copper and throw flowers at it, in guise and with incense, are like butchers sharing out a goat, and asks what worship that is. Both deny that flower-puja reaches the Lord; Sivavakkiyar adds the butcher's comparison and the collected copper, making the rite trade as well as show.

Tirumanthiram 1852 says worship offered where moon and sun shine goes to the asuras, and worship where they do not shine is the great worship of Nandi. 1160 says those who melt the line beyond sun and moon into the one letter in the void are not born again. Both place the goal beyond the sun and moon, which yogic tradition takes as the two side channels; Tirumular speaks of worship, Sivavakkiyar of the end of birth.

Tirumanthiram 890 says the ground at the root is the heat and is நமசிவாய, and the yoga of that ground is the breath. 1162 places the uttered mantra in the chamber of the muladhara, at the seat of seed and blood, and says it is truly Sivayam. Both make the lowest centre the place where the five letters sound; Sivavakkiyar names the generative fluids there outright where Tirumular speaks of heat.

Tirumanthiram 1823 makes the heart the great temple, the body the shrine, the mouth the tower gate, the soul the linga and the five thieving senses the bright lamps. 1163 makes the mind flower and water, the heart the temple, the breath the linga and the five senses incense and lamp. The match is close enough to be a borrowing; Sivavakkiyar changes the linga from soul to breath and adds that the Dancer keeps no hours.

Tirumanthiram 234 says the land where Brahmins live does not decline and its king prospers because they make the oblation at dusk and dawn (அந்தி சந்தி). 1163 says the dancing Lord has no dusk and dawn (அந்தி சந்தி இல்லையே). The conflict holds if 1163 denies that timed rites have any standing; it dissolves if it means only that the inner worship it describes is continuous, leaving outer rites to others.

source_issues: 1140 line 4 அவமைதானது is garbled; உவமை (likeness) or அவள் மேரு may be meant, and the question's object is lost.
1144 line 2 பத்தனாரும் is probably அத்தனாரும் (the Father), as line 4 has அத்தன் ஆடல்.
1150 line 3 மவினஞான for மவுனஞான (line 1) is a spelling slip.
1154 line 3 விண்ணம் cannot be construed; the class sent to hell is lost with it.
1158 line 3 தேடிவத்த for தேடிவந்த is a scribal slip; no change of sense.
